chapters.title: The theme in one minute
paragraphs: In plain words, institutions are the rules that make some actions easy and others hard. They are written rules, such as laws, and unwritten ones, such as what people in an industry take for granted.

Fløysand and colleagues, 2022, take a short definition from North. Institutions are the formal and informal rules that shape action. Then they add a second concept. Institutional work is what actors do to affect those rules.
Why does it matter? Because systems do not change by themselves. Someone has to argue for a new rule, build an organisation, or defend an old arrangement. That work is what this theme studies.

The Norwegian case gives you two kinds of work. In Hordaland, actors worked together across clusters and legitimized a green shift. In Rogaland, leadership stayed individual and the petroleum path held. Same country, same decade, different work.
Remember: institutions are rules, and institutional work is the effort actors spend on those rules.

checks.q: What are institutions, according to the definition the paper borrows?
checks.a: The formal and informal rules that shape action.
The physical and mental work that actors do to affect institutions.

chapters.title: The key ideas
paragraphs: There are four ideas in this theme.
The first is that institutions are rules, but they are also resources. Once a rule exists, it makes some exchanges cheaper, and that is why actors defend it.

The second is that institutional work has four forms. Actors can maintain institutions, create new ones, change existing ones or disrupt them. Maintaining is easy to forget, because it leaves no visible trace.

The third is institutional logics. Fløysand and colleagues, 2022, citing Thornton and Almandoz, describe them as practice patterns and social prescriptions that legitimize practice. A logic tells actors what counts as a proper way to work.

The fourth is the pair of agencies. Following Bækkelund, the same authors separate change agency, which alters a path, from reproductive agency, which keeps a path going. Both are work, and both can be deliberate.

Put the four together. Actors do institutional work inside a logic, and the logic decides whether the work looks legitimate. That is how a green shift can be praised in one region and doubted in another. The same actor can even do both kinds of work at once, defending a cluster while praising a new sector. Listen for that mixture, because it is where the most interesting exam answers live.
Remember: four forms of work, institutional logics, and two kinds of agency.

checks.q: What are the four forms of institutional work?
checks.a: Maintaining, creating, changing and disrupting institutions.
Practice patterns and social prescriptions that legitimize practice.

chapters.title: The model, step by step
paragraphs: There are two models worth knowing.

The first is the four forms of institutional work, and it is easy to hear as a list. First, maintaining institutions, which keeps rules and practices in place. Second, creating institutions, which builds rules that did not exist. Third, changing institutions, which reshapes what is there. Fourth, disrupting institutions, which breaks them down.

The second is the lock-in cycle in Rogaland. Fløysand and colleagues, 2022, report it as a pattern the stakeholders described. A recession lowers costs in the petroleum sector. Then oil prices recover. High profit margins return to the sector. The sector bounces back, and the region stays on its path.
The two models answer different questions. The first tells you what actors can do. The second tells you why they often do the same thing again.
Remember: four forms of work, and a cycle that brings a region back to the same industry.

checks.q: Which form of institutional work leaves no visible trace?
What happens when oil prices recover in Rogaland?
checks.a: High margins return, the sector bounces back and the region stays on its path.

chapters.title: Norway examples
chapters.readings: Fløysand et al. 2022, pp. 15, 22, 25; Class 9, slide 31
paragraphs: The two regions are the main examples, and the details are what make an answer good.
In Hordaland, collective leadership and work across clusters legitimized a green shift. The work was shared, and it drew on a diversified system.
In Rogaland, leadership was individual, and it is linked to Arne Rettedal and the petroleum headquarters in Stavanger. The work concentrated around a few figures and one industry.

The third example is the outcome. Fløysand and colleagues, 2022, say that oil and gas still dominates both regions, unintentionally, despite a shared green vision. That is the finding that makes the theme interesting. Institutional work aimed at a green shift can also help to sustain the old industry.
Remember: collective work in Hordaland, individual leadership in Rogaland, and an outcome nobody intended.

checks.q: What kind of leadership does Rogaland show?
checks.a: Individual leadership, linked to Arne Rettedal and the petroleum headquarters in Stavanger.

checks.q: What is the unintended outcome in both regions?
checks.a: Oil and gas still dominates, despite a shared green vision.

chapters.title: How the exam asks about it
chapters.readings: Fløysand et al. 2022, p. 15; Class 9, slide 31
paragraphs: Two questions fit this theme.

The first is the concept question of June 2025. It asks what you understand by a regional innovation system, institutional work and sustainability. This theme defines the middle term and gives you a case for it.

The second is the discussion question of December 2024, which asks how agency can promote or inhibit sustainable transformation. Institutional work is one form of that agency, so the two themes answer together.

Here is the shape of a good answer. Define institutions as rules. Define institutional work as the effort actors spend on those rules, and name the four forms. Then use the two regions. Say what kind of work legitimized the shift in Hordaland, and what kind kept the path in Rogaland. End with the unintended outcome, because it shows that work can have effects its authors did not plan.
One warning. Do not present institutional work as always progressive. The same concept covers the work that defends an old arrangement, and the exam rewards the student who says so.

There is also a useful sentence about scale. Institutional work happens in a region, but the rules it works on are often national. A regional actor can build a cluster, and it cannot change a tax. A good answer keeps the two levels apart, and says which level the work it describes belongs to. In the Rogaland case, the work sits close to the regional leadership, while the market that keeps petroleum profitable is wider.
Remember: rules, work, four forms, two regions, and an outcome nobody planned.

checks.q: Which two exam questions does this theme serve?
checks.a: The June concept question on institutional work, and the December question on agency.

checks.q: Why should you not call institutional work progressive?
checks.a: Because the same concept covers the work that defends an old arrangement.

chapters.title: Test yourself
paragraphs: Question one. What is the difference between institutions and institutional work?
Pause the audio and answer in your head.
Here is the answer. Institutions are the rules, formal and informal, that shape action. Institutional work is the effort actors spend to maintain, create, change or disrupt those rules.
Question two. What is an institutional logic, and why does it matter for a green shift?
Pause the audio and answer in your head.

Here is the answer. It is a pattern of practice and a set of social prescriptions that legitimize some ways of working. It matters because a green shift needs to look legitimate before actors will commit to it.
Question three. Why do the authors call the outcome in the two regions unintended?
Pause the audio and answer in your head.
Here is the answer. Because the actors in both regions aimed at a green shift, and oil and gas still dominates. The work that sought change also helped to sustain the old industry.
Remember: rules, the work on rules, the logic that makes work legitimate, and outcomes that can surprise their authors.

checks.q: Why keep the regional and national levels apart?
checks.a: Because regional actors can build clusters but cannot change national rules such as taxes.

checks.q: What does the Rogaland case show about the level of the work?
checks.a: The work sits close to regional leadership, while the market that keeps petroleum profitable is wider.
